title: Teen Cannabis Use and Serious Mental Illness
hook: A study of more than 463,000 adolescents tied teen cannabis use to roughly double the risk of serious mental illness — and the use usually came first.
key_points: Study of 463,000+ adolescents linked teen cannabis use to about double the risk of serious mental illness.
The conditions included psychotic and bipolar disorders.
Cannabis use typically preceded the diagnosis by nearly two years.
That timing strengthens concern about effects on the still-developing teenage brain.
It's an observational link, not proof — but the scale and ordering are hard to dismiss.
content_html: Cannabis is often seen as low-risk, but a large study adds weight to a long-standing worry about its use during the teenage years. As ScienceDaily reports, researchers tracking more than 463,000 adolescents found that those who used cannabis faced roughly double the risk of developing serious mental health conditions, including psychotic and bipolar disorders.
extra_html:
What makes the finding more than a simple correlation is the timing: cannabis use typically came first, preceding a diagnosis by nearly two years. When exposure reliably comes before the outcome, it strengthens — though doesn't prove — the case that one may be driving the other. Researchers tie the concern to biology, since the teenage brain is still developing and may be especially vulnerable to substances that act on it.

The usual caveat applies: this is an observational study, so it can't fully rule out that teens prone to mental illness were also more likely to use cannabis for other reasons. But the sheer size of the dataset and the consistent ordering make it hard to wave away. For families, the practical message is that "it's just weed" understates a real risk during a sensitive window of brain development.
